What elementary particle with an antiparticle equivalent has the most equal amount of antiparticles in the Universe?

If I understand your question correctly, you're asking which particle is the closest to a 50/50 split, i.e. for every particle there is a corresponding antiparticle somewhere in the universe. You're probably aware that matter is vastly more common than antimatter, so the balance is never going to be anywhere close to 50/50. Because of that asymmetry, the question boils down to which particle is the least common and which antiparticle is the most common. (It's also possible that neutrinos and antineutrinos are the same, which would make them "balanced" in the sense that each particle qualifies as both matter and antimatter.)

The latter question is easy to answer: positrons. Positrons are readily produced by radioactive beta decay and are also detectable in cosmic rays. As for which particular particle of matter is the least common in comparison with the number of antiparticles, I can't say for sure because I'm not familiar enough with the Standard Model. I feel pretty confident saying that the answer to your question is electrons and positrons, though.
